newsitem.title: USA: SmithKline dampens U.S. drug earnings party.
newsitem.headline: SmithKline dampens U.S. drug earnings party.

text.p: SmithKline Beecham Plc spoiled the earnings party Tuesday for Bristol-Myers Squibb Co and Warner-Lambert Co by announcing it will launch an anticholesterol drug in the U.S. early next year.
Bristol-Myers was off 2-1/2 to 81-11/16 in afternoon trade despite its release earlier in the day of solid second quarter 1997 earnings that matched Wall Street expectations.
And Warner-Lambert was down 3/8 to 139-1/8 despite posting dazzling sales gains for the quarter on Tuesday and handily exceeding the First Call consensus analysts' estimate.

Shares of the U.S. drugmakers were hurt by SmithKline's statement from its London headquarters that it had agreed to co-market Bayer AG's new cholesterol-lowering compound, Baycol, in the U.S. by early 1998.
SmithKline said it would provide marketing and sales support for Baycol, with the two companies sharing revenues from the development of new dosage formulas.
The drug, also known as cerivastatin sodium, was cleared for marketing in June by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

Analysts said SmithKline's entry into the U.S. market could create pricing pressures for Warner-Lambert's anti-cholesterol drug Lipitor, launched just five months ago but expected to rack up sales of over $600 million in 1997.

SmithKline's product is also deemed a potential threat to Bristol-Myers' flagship drug Pravachol, a cholesterol fighter whose worldwide sales jumped 21 percent in the second quarter to $307 million despite Lipitor's noisy arrival on the scene.
"People are concerned SmithKline may come in and demolish pricing for the cholesterol market," said Hambrecht & Quist pharmaceuticals analyst Alex Zisson.
Zisson said SmithKline's drug would be the sixth anti-cholesterol product on the U.S. market and the British company would likely use pricing as a means of muscling its way into the lucrative niche.
"When you're sixth in a market, price can be your biggest weapon," he said.

Merck & Co's Zocor leads the anti-cholesterol pack, with about 27 percent of new U.S. prescription sales. The company reported its second quarter 1997 earnings last week, noting Zocor sales jumped 25 percent to $865 million during the quarter.
Merck's shares treaded negative territory most of the day but edged up 1/4 to 105 midafternoon Tuesday -- restrained by the SmithKline news, analysts said.
Two other U.S.-based companies, American Home Products Corp and Schering-Plough Corp, meanwhile saw their shares rise Tuesday following their release earlier in the day of cheerful earnings results.
American Home Products was up 1-5/16 to 79-3/4. It said earnings per share for the 1997 second quarter rose 15 percent to $0.71, matching the First Call consensus estimate.
Schering-Plough was up 1-1/4 to 50. Its $0.51 earnings-per share figure for the 1997 second quarter was one cent above First Call projections, with year-on-year net earnings rising 18 percent.
Warner-Lambert had reported earnings per share of $0.85 in the recent second quarter, leapfrogging the First Call estimate of $0.81. Sales rose 10 percent, led by Lipitor's $151 million contribution.
Bristol-Myers said its 1997 second quarter earnings per share rose 14 percent to $0.74, matching the First Call consensus estimate.
